title: Ferry bookings that did not get their deck
prompt:
A ferry operator records the deck each passenger asked for and the deck the crew actually assigned. Either column can be NULL: a NULL requested_deck means "no preference", a NULL assigned_deck means "not assigned yet".

The purser wants every booking where the assignment differs from the request. Two NULLs count as the same; a NULL on one side and a deck on the other counts as different.

- Columns: id, passenger, requested_deck, assigned_deck
- Any row order is fine
- Deck names compare exactly (case-sensitive)
hints: What does requested_deck <> assigned_deck return when one side is NULL? Does WHERE keep that row?
Postgres has a comparison operator that treats NULL as an ordinary value.
WHERE requested_deck IS DISTINCT FROM assigned_deck is true for 'a' vs NULL and false for NULL vs NULL.

exercise.schema: CREATE TABLE bookings (id int PRIMARY KEY, passenger text NOT NULL, requested_deck text, assigned_deck text);
exercise.starter:
-- Bookings whose assigned deck differs from the request
SELECT id, passenger, requested_deck, assigned_deck
FROM bookings
WHERE requested_deck <> assigned_deck;

tests.name: mixed bookings
tests.seed: INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (1, 'Ines', 'upper', 'upper'), (2, 'Joe', 'upper', 'lower'), (3, 'Kai', NULL, 'lower'), (4, 'Lea', NULL, NULL);

hiddenTests.name: request made but not yet assigned
both sides NULL only
hiddenTests.seed: INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (1, 'Ed', NULL, NULL), (2, 'Flo', NULL, NULL);

explanation: Plain <> follows SQL's three-valued logic: if either side is NULL the result is NULL, and WHERE drops NULL just like false. That silently hides every unassigned booking and every passenger with no preference who got a deck. IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a comparable value, so NULL vs 'lower' is true and NULL vs NULL is false, which is exactly the rule in the prompt. Writing (a <> b OR (a IS NULL) <> (b IS NULL)) also works but is easy to get wrong.
notes: IS DISTINCT FROM is not indexable as a join or filter condition in the way = is, so on a big table this is a sequential scan; that is fine for a column-vs-column check on the same row. COALESCE(requested_deck, '') <> COALESCE(assigned_deck, '') looks similar but breaks if '' is a real value. IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the NULL-safe equality you would use in a join.
followUps: How would you join two tables on a nullable column so NULL matches NULL?
Why is COALESCE(a, '') = COALESCE(b, '') a risky substitute?
